rows.a: Electrical discharge machining is widely used for nickel-based superalloys such as Hastelloy, which are difficult to cut by conventional means. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Shastri et al. 2022) The choice of electrode material therefore strongly influences both the economic and technical outcomes of EDM: the physical and mechanical properties of the tool electrode affect process efficiency, machining accuracy, and the surface roughness of the machined part. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Electrode wear is one of the main concerns in EDM because high tool wear rates reduce tool life, modify electrode geometry during machining, and can degrade dimensional accuracy and feature quality. (Shastri et al. 2022)(Ramabalan et al. 2024) Surface integrity after machining is the second concern this review examines, since EDM can alter the workpiece surface (including roughness and recast layers), and these changes determine functional performance and may require post-processing. (Shastri et al. 2022)(Liew et al. 2020)
rows.b:
Electrical discharge machining is widely used for nickel‑based superalloys such as Hastelloy because these alloys are difficult to machine by conventional methods; in EDM the workpiece material is removed by electrical discharges between the workpiece and a tool electrode. (Nowicki et al. 2022) (Nowicki et al. 2024) The physical and mechanical properties of the electrode therefore directly influence process efficiency, machining accuracy, and the surface roughness of the machined part. (Nowicki et al. 2022) (Nowicki et al. 2024) Electrode selection thus affects both the economic cost (through tool consumption) and the functional quality of the finished surface (through roughness and integrity). (Nowicki et al. 2022) (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Electrode wear is a primary concern because it alters electrode geometry, degrades dimensional accuracy, and increases tooling costs. (Shastri et al. 2022) Experimental studies on Hastelloy C‑22 using graphite electrodes report systematic effects of electrode microstructure: coarser‑grained graphite provides higher material removal rates but results in greater relative tool wear, whereas finer‑grained graphite tends to produce lower surface roughness and, in some reports, reduced tool wear and increased process efficiency. (Nowicki et al. 2022) (Nowicki et al. 2024) The mechanism proposed for these observations is that graphite grains can detach from the electrode surface during discharge; detached grains modify discharge stability and thus influence removal efficiency and wear behaviour. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

Process parameters mediate these material‑dependent effects. Studies identify peak/discharge current and pulse duration as the dominant drivers of material removal rate and average surface roughness, and the time interval (off‑time) as a dominant factor for relative electrode wear in graphite electrodes on Hastelloy. (Nowicki et al. 2022) (Nas & Kara 2022) Published work on other Hastelloy grades also shows that current and pulse duration strongly affect electrode wear patterns and end‑form evolution (for example, transformation of sharp electrode edges into hemispherical shapes due to unstable sparking and heat diffusion). (Ramabalan et al. 2024) (Shastri et al. 2022)

Surface integrity after EDM—encompassing surface roughness, recast layer characteristics, and subsurface damage—is the second major concern because it determines component performance in hostile environments. (Shastri et al. 2022) Approaches to improve EDM outcomes reported in the literature include process variants and adjunct techniques such as cryogenic treatment of the workpiece, powder‑mixed dielectric, ultrasonic assistance, and combined process improvements; these are investigated for their effects on MRR, TWR, surface roughness, and recast layer formation. (Shastri et al. 2022) (Nas & Kara 2022)

Collectively, the reviewed studies on Hastelloy show consistent links among electrode material and microstructure, machining parameters (notably current and pulse duration), discharge stability, and the twin outcomes of tool wear and surface integrity. (Nowicki et al. 2022) (Nowicki et al. 2024) (Ramabalan et al. 2024) (Shastri et al. 2022) Mathematical and empirical models have been developed in some of these studies to predict machining effects and to guide parameter selection for trade‑offs among process efficiency, tool wear rate, and surface roughness. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

rows.a: Electrical discharge machining is widely used for nickel-based superalloys such as Hastelloy, which are difficult to cut by conventional means. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Shastri et al. 2022) The choice of electrode material therefore influences multiple aspects of the EDM process: the process efficiency, machining accuracy, and the resulting surface roughness are directly linked to the physical and mechanical properties of the tool electrode. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024) As a consequence, electrode material selection affects both the economic cost of machining—through tool consumption and process throughput—and the functional quality of the machined part—through dimensional fidelity and surface condition. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024) Electrode wear is one of the main concerns in EDM because high tool wear reduces electrode life, alters electrode geometry during machining, and can degrade dimensional accuracy and process stability. (Shastri et al. 2022)(Ramabalan et al. 2024) Surface integrity after machining is the second concern this review examines, since the EDM process parameters and electrode characteristics determine surface roughness, recast layer formation, and other surface attributes that affect component performance. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Shastri et al. 2022) Recent work has highlighted a trend toward using graphite electrodes and investigating their microstructure—specifically grain size—because variations in graphite grain size influence material removal effectiveness, relative tool wear rate, and the development of surface roughness on Hastelloy. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)
rows.b:
Electrical discharge machining is widely used for nickel-based superalloys such as Hastelloy because these alloys are difficult to machine by conventional means; in EDM the workpiece material is removed by electrical discharges between the workpiece and the tool electrode, so EDM provides a route to manufacture complex shapes from these materials. (Nowicki et al. 2022) 

The choice of electrode material shapes both the cost and the quality of the process because the physical and mechanical properties of the electrode material directly affect process efficiency, machining accuracy, and surface roughness. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Graphite has seen increased use as an electrode material owing to its low purchase cost, good machinability, and high sublimation temperature, properties that influence both economic and technical outcomes. (Nowicki et al. 2022) 

Electrode wear is one of the main concerns in EDM for nickel-based superalloys because wear alters electrode geometry and therefore accuracy and repeatability; tool wear manifests as changes in electrode shape driven by repeated thermal effects from the spark, with unstable sparks and heat diffusion capable of transforming sharp electrode features into rounded or hemispherical ends. (Ramabalan et al. 2024) The EDM literature identifies high tool wear rate, together with low material removal rate and high surface roughness, as central challenges and motivates combined process variants—such as cryogenic treatment, powder-mixed EDM, ultrasonic assistance, and others—to mitigate these effects. (Shastri et al. 2022) 

Surface integrity after machining is the second concern examined in this review because the electrode material and process parameters determine the machined surface texture and subsurface condition; experimental studies therefore quantify surface roughness (Ra) alongside material removal rate (MRR) and tool wear rate (TWR) to characterise process outcomes. (Nowicki et al. 2022) 

Empirical studies identify the primary process drivers and show how they interact with electrode material properties: discharge current (peak current) and pulse duration (pulse-on time) are reported as the main factors controlling MRR and Ra in graphite electrodes, with statistical analyses (ANOVA, Taguchi methods) attributing the largest shares of effect to peak current in determining both surface roughness and MRR in superalloy EDM experiments. (Nowicki et al. 2022) (Nas & Kara 2022) 

Comparative experiments on graphite electrode grain size report differing but specific effects: one study found that larger-grain graphite (10 µm) provided higher process efficiency (higher MRR) but induced higher relative tool wear, while smaller-grain graphite (1 µm) produced the lowest surface roughness (Ra), and identified discharge current and pulse duration as the dominant parameters for MRR and Ra while the time interval dominated relative tool wear for both graphite grades. (Nowicki et al. 2022) Another study by the same group reports that fine-grained graphite electrodes increase process efficiency and reduce tool wear, and further explains that graphite grains detached from the electrode affect the stability of electrical discharges and thus process efficiency. (Nowicki et al. 2024) 

These findings link mechanisms to measured outcomes: grain detachment from the electrode alters discharge stability and therefore the material-removal mechanism and efficiency, while current and pulse duration control the thermal energy per discharge that determines both MRR and the surface texture produced. (Nowicki et al. 2024) (Nowicki et al. 2022)

rows.a: Selective laser melting (SLM) builds components layer-by-layer by selectively melting metallic powders with a high-power laser, enabling near–net-shape, near–full-density parts with complex geometries directly from powder feedstock (Yap et al. 2015)(Haghdadi et al. 2020). Post-print heat treatments—such as solution treatment, aging, intercritical tempering, and combined thermochemical treatments like plasma nitriding—alter the as-built microstructure by modifying precipitate populations, relieving residual stresses, and inducing phase changes such as reversed austenite formation and martensitic tempering (Godec et al. 2021)(Tan et al. 2018)(Khan et al. 2022)(Haghdadi et al. 2020). While many studies have focused on achieving and explaining enhanced mechanical properties (for example through precipitation hardening, martensite-to-austenite reversion, and the mitigation of residual stresses), investigations specifically addressing how these microstructural changes affect corrosion behaviour—particularly in chloride environments—are comparatively limited, and the influence of treatments that improve mechanical performance on corrosion resistance is not yet fully understood (Tan et al. 2018)(Khan et al. 2022)(Afkhami et al. 2019)(Haghdadi et al. 2020). Studies that do examine corrosion aspects report varied approaches and outcomes—for example, work on nitriding and on the role of reversed austenite indicate that prior heat treatments and local chemistry can significantly influence corrosion and pitting resistance—but a comprehensive understanding linking SLM processing, subsequent heat treatments, and corrosion performance remains incomplete (Godec et al. 2021)(Khan et al. 2022).
rows.b: Selective laser melting (SLM) produces parts by selectively melting and fusing metal powder in a layerwise fashion, enabling near-net-shape fabrication of dense, geometrically complex components directly from powder feedstock. (Yap et al. 2015) (Haghdadi et al. 2020) The SLM process’s very high solidification rates lead to unique as-built microstructures—extremely fine submicron grains and in situ precipitation—that differ from conventionally manufactured maraging steels and underpin distinctly different mechanical and corrosion-relevant behaviour. (Tan et al. 2018) (Haghdadi et al. 2020) Post-build heat treatments substantially modify these as-built microstructures: solution treatment, aging, and intercritical tempering change precipitate populations (for example, Ni3X needle-shaped nanoprecipitates responsible for age hardening), relieve residual stresses, alter mechanical anisotropy, and can induce martensite-to-austenite reversion depending on temperature and prior condition. (Tan et al. 2018) (Khan et al. 2022) Thermochemical surface treatments such as plasma nitriding interact with prior heat treatments; for instance, nitriding without prior aging led to defects in the compound layer, whereas nitriding after heat treatment improved wear and corrosion resistance in additive-manufactured 18Ni-300. (Godec et al. 2021) The mechanisms linking heat treatment to corrosion behaviour include precipitate dissolution and local elemental redistribution (e.g., Ni enrichment) that can nucleate reversed austenite along martensite lath boundaries and thereby influence pitting resistance in chloride media. (Khan et al. 2022) Despite several studies addressing mechanical properties and tailored heat treatments, the effect of these microstructural changes on corrosion—particularly in chloride environments—remains comparatively less explored, with reviews and recent studies highlighting gaps in understanding of fatigue, ductility, and the corrosion implications of AM-specific microstructures. (Afkhami et al. 2019) (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

rows.a: Mobile health applications for diabetes self-management have proliferated alongside the rapid global uptake of smartphones, with tens of thousands of health-related apps available on major platforms by the mid-2010s. (Zhao et al. 2016) A range of evaluations and trials have examined whether these apps affect self-management behaviors and clinical outcomes such as glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c); pilot studies and randomized trials report measures of blood‑glucose monitoring frequency and HbA1c as outcomes. (Cafazzo et al. 2012)(Agarwal et al. 2018) Trial results are mixed: some app-based interventions have been associated with increased self-monitoring or small usage-related improvements, while pragmatic randomized data have not shown clear overall effects on HbA1c at primary endpoints. (Cafazzo et al. 2012)(Agarwal et al. 2018) Measured app engagement is often limited and variable across settings, with usage tending to decline after the initial weeks and with site- and context-specific factors influencing sustained use. (Peng et al. 2016)(Agarwal et al. 2018)
rows.b:
Mobile health applications have been proposed as a low‑cost means to support diabetes self‑management, in the context of a large and growing market of health apps and concern about variability in app quality, usability, and connectivity standards. (Boulos et al. 2014)(Zhao et al. 2016) 

Their effect on glycaemic control has been measured in several trials and evaluations with mixed results. A multicentre pragmatic randomized controlled trial of the BlueStar app found no difference between intervention and control arms for the primary outcome of HbA1c at 3 months (adjusted mean difference −0.42, 95% CI −1.05 to 0.21; P=.19). (Agarwal et al. 2018) However, exploratory analyses in the same trial indicated a dose–response relation between app use and glycaemic change: each additional day of app use was associated with a 0.016‑point decrease in 3‑month HbA1c (95% CI −0.03 to −0.003), suggesting that sufficient and sustained engagement may be required to translate app use into clinical benefit. (Agarwal et al. 2018) Smaller pilot work using gamification and automated device connectivity (in adolescents with type 1 diabetes) showed a 50% increase in daily blood glucose measurements (from 2.4 to 3.6 per day, P =.006, n = 12), indicating that specific design features can change self‑monitoring behaviour even when improvements in HbA1c would require longer or larger studies to demonstrate. (Cafazzo et al. 2012) Systematic reviews of mobile app interventions for health behaviours report that most included studies (17/23) observed statistically significant behaviour change, but that study quality is variable and risk of bias is present, so conclusions about clinical outcomes remain provisional. (Zhao et al. 2016) 

Engagement tends to fall after the first weeks of use, and this decline helps explain heterogeneous trial results. Reported retention in app interventions varies widely (60%–100% in the review), and qualitative work identifies multiple barriers to continued use—such as perceived time burden, lack of personalised guidance, limited credibility, inadequate goal‑setting or reminders, and concerns about sharing personal information—while motivators include tracking for awareness, personalised feedback, and social or reward mechanisms. (Zhao et al. 2016)(Peng et al. 2016) Empirical app‑usage data from trials show large between‑site variation in median days of use over 14 weeks (for example, medians of 36 days [IQR 10.5–124] versus 9 days [IQR 6–51] at different sites), indicating that context and implementation strongly influence sustained engagement. (Agarwal et al. 2018) In combination, these findings point to mechanisms by which apps can influence glycaemic control—principally through self‑monitoring, real‑time feedback, individualised content, clinician involvement, and behaviour‑change techniques—but also to the conditions required for those mechanisms to operate (adequate duration of use, high usability, contextual support, and trustworthy app quality). (Zhao et al. 2016)(Cafazzo et al. 2012)(Boulos et al. 2014)

(Khan et al. 2022) (Huis et al. 2017) The effectiveness of microfinance in producing sustained empowerment depends on intervention design, timing, cultural context, and the institutional model through which services are delivered; market pressures and the mix of commercial and subsidized institutions also shape who benefits.
